Ridge Regression with ridge

Mustapha Labhar

Source: vignettes/ridge.Rmd
ridge.Rmd

Introduction

The ridge package provides tools for fitting and working with ridge regression models. It includes model fitting, cross-validation for selecting the regularization parameter, graphical visualization of cross-validation errors, and prediction methods.

This vignette presents a complete and reproducible workflow using the main functions and S3 methods implemented in the package.

The Ridge Regression Model

Ridge regression is a regularized linear regression method designed to reduce the magnitude of regression coefficients.

The estimator minimizes the following penalized least-squares criterion:

β̂λ=argminβ[∑i=1n(yi−β0−xi⊤β)2+λ∑j=1pβj2]. \widehat{\beta}_{\lambda} = \arg\min_{\beta} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i-\beta_0-x_i^\top\beta)^2 + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2 \right].

Here, λ\lambda controls the strength of regularization. A larger value of λ\lambda produces stronger shrinkage of the explanatory-variable coefficients.

The intercept is not penalized in the implementation used by this package.

Generating a Reproducible Dataset

We generate a simulated dataset with two explanatory variables and a known underlying linear relationship.

set.seed(123)

x <- matrix(rnorm(200), ncol = 2)
colnames(x) <- c("x1", "x2")

y <- 2 + 3 * x[, 1] - x[, 2] + rnorm(100)

The data-generating process is:

Yi=2+3Xi1−Xi2+εi, Y_i = 2 + 3X_{i1} - X_{i2} + \varepsilon_i,

where the error term follows a standard normal distribution.

The theoretical coefficients are therefore 2 for the intercept, 3 for the first explanatory variable, and -1 for the second.

Fitting a Ridge Model

The ridge_fit() function fits a ridge regression model for a specified regularization parameter.

library(ridge)

model <- ridge_fit(
  x = x,
  y = y,
  lambda = 1
)

model
#> Ridge Regression Model
#> ----------------------
#> Lambda: 1 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> (Intercept)          x1          x2 
#>   2.1390816   2.8329507  -0.9673232
coef(model)
#> (Intercept)          x1          x2 
#>   2.1390816   2.8329507  -0.9673232

The resulting object belongs to the S3 class ridge_model.

The estimated coefficients can be compared with the theoretical values used to generate the data.

head(fitted(model))
#> [1] 1.238475 1.238511 6.793456 2.675014 3.425870 7.041333
head(residuals(model))
#> [1]  1.9893154  1.1264862 -0.1357845  0.4272474 -0.5007284 -0.3273568

Cross-Validation

The ridge_cv() function performs k-fold cross-validation over a user-defined grid of regularization parameters.

We consider 50 values of lambda distributed on a logarithmic scale.

lambda_grid <- 10^seq(-3, 2, length.out = 50)

cv_result <- ridge_cv(
  x = x,
  y = y,
  lambda_grid = lambda_grid,
  k = 5,
  seed = 123
)

cv_result$best_lambda
#> [1] 0.08685114
cv_result$best_mse
#> [1] 0.9270251

The selected parameter minimizes the estimated mean cross-validation error over the specified grid.

Visualizing Cross-Validation Errors

The S3 plotting method displays the mean cross-validation error as a function of lambda, together with its standard error and the selected regularization parameters.

selected_parameters <- plot(cv_result)


selected_parameters
#>    lambda_min    lambda_1se     min_error        se_min threshold_1se 
#>    0.08685114    7.54312006    0.92702508    0.08993552    1.01696061

Two selection criteria are considered:

  • The minimum-error criterion selects the lambda associated with the smallest estimated cross-validation error.
  • The one-standard-error rule selects the largest lambda whose estimated error remains within one standard error of the minimum.

The latter favors stronger regularization while accepting a cross-validation error close to the minimum.

Comparing the Selected Models

We fit two models using the parameters selected by the two criteria.

model_min <- ridge_fit(
  x = x,
  y = y,
  lambda = selected_parameters["lambda_min"]
)

model_1se <- ridge_fit(
  x = x,
  y = y,
  lambda = selected_parameters["lambda_1se"]
)

comparison <- cbind(
  Theoretical = c(2, 3, -1),
  Lambda_min = coef(model_min),
  Lambda_1se = coef(model_1se)
)

comparison
#>             Theoretical Lambda_min Lambda_1se
#> (Intercept)           2  2.1354178  2.1633122
#> x1                    3  2.8638539  2.6296842
#> x2                   -1 -0.9754127 -0.9128905

The Euclidean norms of the explanatory-variable coefficients can be used to illustrate the shrinkage induced by regularization.

beta_min <- coef(model_min)[-1]
beta_1se <- coef(model_1se)[-1]

sqrt(sum(beta_min^2))
#> [1] 3.025407
sqrt(sum(beta_1se^2))
#> [1] 2.783632

Prediction

The predict() method allows predictions to be obtained for new observations.

newdata <- x[1:5, , drop = FALSE]

predict(model, newdata = newdata)
#> [1] 1.238475 1.238511 6.793456 2.675014 3.425870

We can also compare the training mean squared errors of the two selected models.

pred_min <- predict(model_min, newdata = x)
pred_1se <- predict(model_1se, newdata = x)

mse_min <- mean((y - pred_min)^2)
mse_1se <- mean((y - pred_1se)^2)

data.frame(
  Model = c("Minimum CV", "One-standard-error rule"),
  Lambda = c(
    selected_parameters["lambda_min"],
    selected_parameters["lambda_1se"]
  ),
  Training_MSE = c(mse_min, mse_1se)
)
#>                              Model     Lambda Training_MSE
#> lambda_min              Minimum CV 0.08685114    0.8778267
#> lambda_1se One-standard-error rule 7.54312006    0.9292174

These training errors describe the fit on the observations used for model estimation. They should not be interpreted as independent estimates of predictive performance.

Conclusion

The ridge package provides a workflow for fitting ridge regression models, selecting regularization parameters through cross-validation, visualizing validation errors, and generating predictions.

The minimum-error and one-standard-error criteria provide different regularization choices. Their comparison illustrates the relationship between coefficient shrinkage and model fit.

The examples in this vignette are reproducible and use a simulated dataset with known theoretical coefficients.
